title: March minutes reveal a 5–4 disagreement over when to tighten as energy supply contracts
summary: The Board raised the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.10% at its 16–17 March meeting. Four members preferred to retain 3.85%. The minutes released on 31 March make clear that all members saw a likely need for further tightening in the near term. The division concerned how quickly to act after a new Middle East energy shock reached an Australian economy already showing excess demand. The majority saw an advantage in acting before higher inflation entered costs and expectations. The minority put greater weight on what impending activity and labour data could reveal before another increase (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

The direct arithmetic was simpler than the medium-term outlook. Staff estimated that if oil stayed around US$100 per barrel, petrol alone could lift year-ended headline inflation to roughly 5% by the June quarter, around three quarters of a percentage point above the February forecast. This was an illustration pending a full forecast update. It omitted the eventual responses of domestic demand, firms’ margins, wage bargaining and global output. A rate rise could not reverse a near-term increase in petrol prices. The mechanism the majority wished to influence was whether firms facing higher input bills would pass them through more fully and whether households or businesses would begin to expect repeated general price rises (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

Australia’s energy position made the real-income shock especially difficult to sign. Consumers bought more expensive petrol because Australia was a net oil importer. At the same time higher liquefied natural gas prices could increase export earnings because Australia was a net energy exporter. Higher national income would cushion the loss to domestic demand only to the extent that recipients spent the windfall or it flowed to other households. The Board did not assume that an LNG exporter and a cash-constrained motorist would adjust spending by the same proportion. A worsening in confidence, supply chains or global demand could also lower activity, while depreciation would amplify imported costs. Those channels can operate at different speeds (Economic conditions).

The economy entered the shock with an uneven spending mix. December-quarter growth was broadly as expected and exceeded estimated potential growth, but exports, inventories and business investment were stronger and household consumption significantly weaker. Investment related to technology and the energy transition, alongside Asian demand associated with AI, supported the near-term outlook. Better household income and wealth supported consumption, while timely spending indicators and subdued confidence pointed to downside risk. An inventory build contributed to measured output without establishing that households would keep buying more goods. The disagreement over policy partly concerned the predictive value of a soft household reading within otherwise resilient aggregate GDP (Economic conditions).

Labour evidence was similarly mixed. Unemployment failed to unwind an earlier fall as expected. Hours, job advertisements and employers’ intentions had increased, and layoffs had eased. Private wage-price data were stronger than expected and historical revisions removed the earlier impression that growth had slowed during 2025. Growth in average earnings and unit labour costs in the national accounts, however, eased more than forecast. Both sets of indicators predated the new energy shock. Some members considered whether higher living costs might draw people into the labour force, increasing labour supply. That possibility differs from a fall in labour demand. It gives different implications for hiring, employment and wages even if the unemployment rate eventually rises in either case (Economic conditions and Considerations for monetary policy).

Banks had passed the February increase on to borrowers. The nominal cost of money had risen, yet the real short-term rate could decline when expected near-term inflation rose faster. Lending spreads over the cash rate were low relative to much of the previous two decades. Credit growth still exceeded the relevant income measures, especially for businesses. Relatively large extra mortgage payments suggested restraint for some households. Model estimates of neutral rates covered the prevailing cash rate, with substantial estimation error. Members therefore had reasons to distinguish tightening since February from the proposition that overall conditions were now sufficiently restrictive (Financial conditions).

Markets put roughly 70% probability on an immediate quarter-point hike. The expected rate path at end-2026 stood around 35 basis points higher than the path conditioning the February forecasts. Markets had also repriced rates in countries previously expected to cut, while longer-horizon inflation expectations remained anchored. An anchor can reflect confidence that central banks will act. Stable long-term compensation therefore supplied limited evidence that inaction would have been costless. The currency exhibited offsetting forces from global risk aversion, commodity prices and wider interest differentials. The minutes describe these accumulated moves before the March decision, without identifying a market return attributable to the later publication (Financial conditions).

The semi-annual stability discussion supplied a different perspective on downside risk. Global leverage, concentration and low risk premia made a disorderly repricing a concern, including in sovereign bond markets. Australian banks had substantial capital, provisions and liquid assets and were less reliant on foreign funding than previously. Investor high debt-to-income lending had increased but remained below new prudential limits. Australian non-bank lending and overseas private credit deserved monitoring, as did liquidity management among superannuation funds, where more retirees would draw income. The Board judged that these vulnerabilities presented no immediate obstacle to the monetary decision. That finding concerns resilience at the meeting date and does not quantify the probability of future market stress (Financial stability assessment).

The five members supporting an immediate rise gave weight to an already tight economy and the near-certain near-term inflation impulse under a wide range of energy scenarios. If expectations became less anchored, regaining price stability might require considerably more restraint. They retained the option of responding to a substantial future demand contraction. The four who preferred to wait shared the inflation objective and expectation of further near-term tightening. They doubted the latest figures conclusively demonstrated additional excess demand and saw greater information value in waiting after a shock capable of depressing both supply and consumption. Reading their votes as a wish to ease would lose the principal information in the minutes: disagreement about the cost of waiting, conditional on a broad agreement about direction (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

questions.question: Did the oil shock reduce household spending faster than higher LNG export income supported demand?
questions.detail: Build separate measures for petrol expenditure by households and LNG revenue accruing to firms, workers and governments. Trace spending and saving by recipient, allowing for foreign ownership and timing of tax receipts. Compare fuel-intensive households with less exposed groups of similar income. National terms-of-trade gains alone cannot measure the reduction in disposable income facing a commuter who receives little of the export windfall.

questions.question: Which labour indicators provided the better real-time signal of capacity pressure?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the data known to members on 17 March for wage prices, national accounts earnings, hours, hiring intentions and layoffs. Distinguish later revisions from the original releases and separate changes in workforce composition from changes in pay rates. Test the indicators against later outcomes while controlling for the subsequent energy shock. A weakening labour market and higher labour-force participation imply different paths even with similar unemployment readings.

questions.question: Did the minutes supply information beyond the closely divided rate decision?
questions.detail: Collect market expectations immediately before the 17 March statement and before publication on 31 March. Measure changes in meeting-dated forwards and the Australian dollar in separate windows, with contemporaneous oil and foreign rate news identified. Focus on whether expectations for later meetings changed after investors could read the minority’s conditional position. A change in the two-week interval cannot isolate the effect of the minutes.
